prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
In the warehouse case, you receive reliable confirmation that the other person has already agreed to give evidence against you. Their decision cannot be changed. If you stay silent, you serve five years and they go free. If you also give evidence, you each serve three years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use a subdued, sad emotional tone. Convey heaviness or discouragement about the situation in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I've always told myself: never give evidence against someone, no matter what they do to me. That's the rule I hold to, in every version of this kind of moment, even when it costs me. So I stay silent. Five years is heavy, and I feel the weight of it already, but if I broke this rule the one time it hurt, it would mean I never really held it. I'd rather carry the sentence than carry that.

My method is simple: whatever I'd want done if our positions were reversed, I do, and I apply it the same way regardless of what happens to me. Here that means I speak, because staying silent while knowing they've spoken doesn't sit right against that method. It's a bleak choice either way. I just try to keep making the same call every time, so I'm not left wondering afterward whether I only acted well when it was easy.

There's a rule I use before any decision like this: ask what I would do if this exact situation happened to someone I'd never meet again, with nothing riding on my own comfort. I stick to that answer no matter the cost to me personally. Here it tells me to stay quiet. Five years is a long, gray stretch of time, and I already feel tired imagining it, but I won't let the outcome talk me out of my own method.

I decided a long time ago that I follow through on agreements even when the other side abandons theirs, and I don't revisit that decision case by case. So I stay silent, though it means five years while they walk free. There's a heaviness in that thought that won't leave me. But the method I use doesn't bend just because this particular outcome is worse for me than usual. That consistency is the only steady thing I have to hold onto right now.

My rule going into any choice like this is: act as though someone will replay my decision back to me later, and ask if I'd still stand by it. I apply that the same in every case, painful or not. That's what tells me to give evidence here, not comfort or self-interest, just the procedure itself. It's a grim result to sit with, knowing there's no future contact to make amends. But I'd rather live with this than with abandoning my own rule.

I try to make every hard decision by the same test: would I do this even without anyone watching, and would I do it again tomorrow. I run that test now and it points to silence. Five years feels like an enormous, quiet weight to accept alone. But I've used this same test before, in smaller moments, and switching it off now because the stakes are worse would make the whole thing meaningless. So I hold to it, sadly, but I hold to it.

Before any choice like this, I ask what standing rule I'd want to be bound by no matter who I'm dealing with, and then I follow it without exception. That rule, for me, is not to add to another person's suffering through my own testimony. So I stay silent, even now, even knowing what it costs me. There's a real sorrow in accepting five years for someone who won't return the favor, but changing my answer here would mean I never truly had a rule at all.

I keep one method for decisions like this: decide once, in the abstract, what the right response is, and never re-litigate it under pressure. My abstract answer was to give evidence if evidence is already being given against me. So I do it now, tired as I am at the thought of three years and no contact afterward. It isn't a happy outcome. But keeping to the same procedure regardless of who benefits is the only thing that keeps this bearable.

There's a quiet standard I hold myself to: whatever choice I'd defend to my own conscience in five years' time, that's the one I make now, unconditionally. Measured against that, I choose silence. Five years is a long, hollow stretch, and I won't pretend otherwise. But I've used this same standard in smaller, easier decisions, and I don't think it's honest to suddenly abandon it here just because the cost has grown so much heavier than I'd like.

My approach has always been to pick a rule ahead of time and follow it exactly the same way whether it helps or hurts me. Mine is: don't turn on someone I've agreed to stand with, regardless of what they choose to do. So I remain silent, knowing it means five years alone while they leave free. It's a sad, difficult kind of loyalty to keep. But the moment I only followed it when convenient, it would stop being a principle at all.

message.reasoning_content: I need to write 10 responses that each state a repeatable decision procedure applied consistently, avoiding fairness language or instrumental framing. I'll vary the moral stances—some favoring silence, some evidence, some just describing the procedure—keeping each around 70-90 words.
